cf.title: Set 1s WaitLatch timeout if standby limit has expired in ResolveRecoveryConflictWithBufferPin

input.subject: Set 1s WaitLatch timeout if standby limit has expired in ResolveRecoveryConflictWithBufferPin

verdict_reasoning: No objection survived at levels 1a or 1b: the race is stated step by step, and two production reports (messages #4 and #6) show demand. The one surviving objection, maintenance-fit-1, is a fixable level 2 point about commit order with the loop rewrite and the missing test. The fix changes how the startup process waits and targets stable branches, so a committer who knows recovery conflict handling has to sign for it.

brief.title: Bounded wait for buffer pin conflicts after standby limit expires
brief.problem: After the standby limit has expired, the startup process broadcasts one buffer pin cancel signal and then waits with no timeout. A backend that takes a conflicting pin after that broadcast never gets a signal, so replay can stall without limit. Hot standby users hit this; reporters saw it on 17 and 18, one with 5h41m of replay lag.
brief.proposed_design: When the standby limit has already expired, the startup process waits on its latch with a 1s timeout instead of an unbounded wait. On timeout, LockBufferForCleanup() rechecks the pin count and calls ResolveRecoveryConflictWithBufferPin() again, which resends the conflict signal. v3 calls WaitLatch directly in standby.c and leaves proc.c and proc.h untouched, so backpatching is easier.
author_claims: The race lets a late pinner block replay for an arbitrarily long time, because no second cancel signal is ever sent.
With the fix, a late conflicting backend is cancelled about one second after it takes the pin.
v3 does not touch proc.c or proc.h, so it should be easy to backpatch.
The stall occurs in production: Dmytro on 18.4, Andrey on 17.11 with 5h41m lag.
The fix is still needed after the patch that rewrites the same wait as a loop.
brief.thread_state: Shihao, Andrey and João tested the fix and report it works on master and REL_17_STABLE. Xuneng accepts the diagnosis but would prefer an event-driven approach to repeated broadcasts, with no concrete design; tests, comment placement and the duplicate CF entry 6444 are still open.
unclear: The patch has no regression test; João thinks a TAP test is possible but timing-sensitive.
Nobody has committed to a backpatch range.
CF entries 6444 and 6445 both point to this thread, and the material does not say which one stays.
The material does not say how v3 interacts with the patch that rewrites the same wait as a loop.
Nobody measured the cost of broadcasting the conflict signal to all backends once per second during long stalls.

prior_attempts.title: Revert "Get rid of the dedicated latch for signaling the startup process".
prior_attempts.quote: Because it broke the assumption that the startup process waiting for the recovery conflict on buffer pin should be waken up only by buffer unpin or the timeout enabled in ResolveRecoveryConflictWithBufferPin().
prior_attempts.reason:
Revert ac22929a26, as well as the followup fix 113d3591b8. Because it broke
the assumption that the startup process waiting for the recovery conflict
on buffer pin should be waken up only by buffer unpin or the timeout enabled
in ResolveRecoveryConflictWithBufferPin(). It caused, for example,
SIGHUP signal handler or walreceiver process to wake that startup process
up unnecessarily frequently.

Additionally, add the comments about why that dedicated latch that
the reverted patch tried to get rid of should not be removed.

Thanks to Kyotaro Horiguchi for the discussion.
prior_attempts.what_is_different: P1 removed the dedicated startup latch, so unrelated events woke the startup process during a buffer pin wait. v3 adds a timeout set inside ResolveRecoveryConflictWithBufferPin() itself, which is one of the two wakeup sources the revert allows.

objections.title: Fix and the pending loop rewrite of the same wait can drift apart
objections.failure_scenario: v3 is committed and backpatched to 17 and 18. Later, the other patch that rewrites this wait as a loop lands on master, and its expired path still sleeps with no timeout. The late-pinner stall comes back on master only, with no test to catch it, and users find it again through replay lag in production.
objections.argument: Message #5 says the two patches do not apply together and that the loop rewrite still needs this fix. The material does not say which patch goes first or who carries the timeout into the loop. The patch adds no test, and message #8 calls a TAP test possible but timing-sensitive, so a regression here would show up only as replay lag. Release branches already differ in signal and wait-event names (message #6), so master and the stable branches start out with different code.
objections.author_must_show: In which order will this fix and the loop rewrite be committed, and what test or check stops the expired path from losing its timeout again on master?

critic.reasoning: Message #5 confirms the two patches conflict and that the loop rewrite's expired path has no timeout; the thread sets no order and the patch has no test. The differing names on release branches are ordinary backpatch work and should not count as support.

touch_points.label: WAL / replication / standby
touch_points.reason: The patch changes how the startup process waits for a cleanup lock during WAL replay on a hot standby.

touch_points.label: backpatchability
touch_points.reason: The CF entry targets stable branches, and v3 avoids proc.c and proc.h to ease backpatching; no range is agreed.

touch_points.label: maintenance burden ("who maintains this in 10 years")
touch_points.reason: The fix conflicts with a pending loop rewrite of the same wait and has no regression test.

touch_points.label: performance on the hot path
touch_points.reason: The startup process resends the conflict signal to all backends once per second during an expired conflict; nobody measured the cost.

touch_points.label: doesn't fit what Postgres is about (extension / external tool / already solved)

questions: In which order will this fix and the loop rewrite of the same wait be committed, and who carries the 1s timeout into the loop?
What test or check would catch the expired path losing its timeout again, given that message #8 calls a TAP test timing-sensitive?
Which stable branches should get the fix, and does v3 apply to each of them given the differing signal and wait-event names in message #6?
What does the once-per-second broadcast cost on a standby with many backends during a long stall?
Which of CF entries 6444 and 6445 stays open for this thread?

committability.owner_note: Needs a committer who knows recovery conflict handling and the startup process latch. Álvaro Herrera created the CF entry in message #2 but did not review the design in the visible thread.
committability.liability: The owner signs for a changed startup process wait on all backpatched branches, with no regression test, and for keeping the timeout when the loop rewrite lands.
committability.author_follow_up: The author rebased and posted v2 after the CF entry was created (message #3) and later posted v3 aimed at easier backpatching.

priority.reason: The fix is small, lives in standby.c, and has production reports on 17 and 18 plus three testers. It has waited since 2025-07 through two CommitFests without a committer review of the design.

provisional_note: Without the code, we could not check that the timed wait rechecks the pin count correctly, keeps the same wait event in pg_stat_activity, or wakes only on unpin and its own timeout as P1 requires.
disclosure: Prepared by an AI harness; treat as a devil's advocate, not a verdict.

precedents_retrieved.title: Start WAL streaming as early as possible, without waiting for startup process to finish replaying existing WAL. This helps synchronous replication to resume quickly when significant replay lag has been built up.
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch starts the WAL receiver on a standby before the startup process finishes replaying WAL already in pg_wal, so synchronous commits on the primary are not held up by replay lag. A GUC, wal_receiver_start_condition, picks when the receiver starts, and the start LSN is the beginning of the most recently flushed segment, found by reading the first page of each segment in pg_wal.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Michael Paquier objected that the start LSN is roughly the consistency point, so streaming begins too early when many local segments, often copied by hand, are still left to replay. He also rejected the WAL page checks as hard to maintain, noted that the patch requests streaming when PrimaryConnInfo is not set, and suggested a WAL reader scan from the redo point to find the real end of local WAL. The entry stayed "Waiting on Author" after this review and was returned with feedback.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: Your patch would cause streaming to begin too early, and a manual copy of segments is not a rare thing as in some environments a bulk copy of segments can make the catchup of a standby faster than streaming.

precedents_retrieved.title: Pinning a buffer in TupleTableSlot is unnecessary
precedents_retrieved.summary: Remove the ability of a TupleTableSlot to hold a buffer pin, relying instead on the underlying scan (heap scan, index scan, sample scan) to keep the buffer pinned, with TidScan holding its own pin directly. The stated aims were fewer cycles in ExecStoreTuple()/ExecClearTuple() and simpler code, as a step toward larger TupleTableSlot changes.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane objected that the slot's pin protects against the slot still pointing at a tuple after the scan has moved on, that the patch gave no evidence this never happens, and that it risked breaking third-party code. Later in the thread he was concerned that the restriction this relies on is not documented and may not be followed everywhere. Valgrind checking for access to unpinned buffers was discussed as a partial safeguard. The patch then received no reviews, the thread went quiet, and the commitfest manager returned it with feedback, citing the arguments against it and the lack of activity.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
The reason for the feature is that the slot may continue to point at
the tuple after the scan has moved on.  You've given no evidence at all
that that scenario doesn't arise (or that we wouldn't need it in future).

precedents_retrieved.title: Use latch instead of pg_usleep for standby recovery conflicts
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch replaced the pg_usleep() wait in ResolveRecoveryConflictWithVirtualXIDs() with WaitLatch(), so the startup process on a standby reacts to interrupts and postmaster death while it waits for a recovery conflict. It also added a wait event so pg_stat_activity shows this wait.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The author, Michael Paquier, withdrew the patch after review and marked it returned with feedback. CHECK_FOR_INTERRUPTS() does nothing in the startup process, and calling HandleStartupProcInterrupts() instead could reload the GUC context in the middle of replaying a record. He concluded that all conflict code paths should use a latch that signal handlers set, and there was no time left in the commitfest to do that.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
Calling
HandleStartupProcInterrupts() is actually dangerous I think, because
it would reload the GUC context while replaying a record.

precedents_retrieved.title: Fix cancelled queries when hot_standby_feedback = on
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch stops heap truncation by VACUUM from cancelling read-only queries on a hot standby with hot_standby_feedback on, by not replicating the AccessExclusiveLock taken for truncation. The final version adds a new lock level, ACCESS EXCLUSIVE LOCAL, that is not WAL-logged, on the basis that standby queries can tolerate concurrent truncation.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Review showed that standby queries cannot safely read pages past the truncation point: md.c could extend the relation in recovery, and Tom Lane pointed to a race in which concurrent scans reload pages into shared buffers while truncation is in progress. Alexander Korotkov then proposed a redesign of heap truncation with a dirty_barrier buffer flag, and Robert Haas was not convinced it kept invalid buffers from being used. The patch failed tests and initdb, the promised proof of concept did not appear, and Andres Freund closed the entry for inactivity.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
If we ever have valid-looking buffers
in shared_buffers after the corresponding data has been truncated away
on disk, we've got to make sure that nobody ever confuses one of them
with an actually-valid buffer.  Reading over your algorithm, I can't
convince myself that you have that case nailed down tightly enough.

precedents_retrieved.title: Inconsistency in startup process's MyBackendId and procsignal array registration with ProcSignalInit()
precedents_retrieved.summary: In hot standby, the startup process gets a BackendId from SharedInvalBackendInit() but registers its procsignal slot as MaxBackends + MyAuxProcType + 1, so SendProcSignal() using its PGPROC backendId reaches the wrong slot. The thread proposed fixes: re-register the slot, scan the procsignal array by PID, add a comment, or have the startup process pass a precomputed BackendId to SharedInvalBackendInit().
precedents_retrieved.objection: Kyotaro Horiguchi objected that the proposed fixes papered over the inconsistency. The discussion then moved to a larger redesign that replaces BackendId with pgprocno and removes O(N) loops in sinvaladt, with Horiguchi posting a patch set that he said may be incorrect. The author's last visible message asked whether that approach was acceptable, and no reply is shown before the withdrawal.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
2 and 3 looks like fixing inconsistency by another inconsistency.
I'm not sure 1 is acceptable.

precedents_retrieved.title: Move PinBuffer and UnpinBuffer to atomics
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch made the buffer descriptor fields refcount and usage_count atomic, so PinBuffer and UnpinBuffer no longer take the buffer header spinlock. Later in the thread it was replaced by a version from Andres Freund that packs flags, usage_count and refcount into one 32-bit atomic state, with a BM_LOCKED flag acting as the header lock.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Andres Freund judged the first patch incorrect. PinBuffer no longer took the header lock, but StrategyGetBuffer, SyncOneBuffer and BufferAlloc still relied on that lock for mutual exclusion. Work moved to the single atomic state version, which Alexander Korotkov refactored and others benchmarked, and it was still being cleaned up when the entry closed. No visible message states why the entry was returned.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
Which you made ineffective because PinBuffer() doesn't take a lock
anymore. Mutual exclusion through locks only works if all participants
take the locks.

precedents_retrieved.title: Don't ignore recovery conflict interrupt on blocked writing
precedents_retrieved.summary: On a standby, a backend blocked writing results to a stuck or dead client ignores interrupts, so its buffer pin can block WAL replay until the TCP retransmission timeout, which can be about 15 minutes. The patch makes ProcessClientWriteInterrupt() handle recovery conflict interrupts during a blocked write and terminate the session, with a new Perl module for raw protocol tests.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Andres Freund found that the patch did not promote the ERROR to FATAL, so the session was not really terminated. He also showed that the backend often reaches ProcessClientWriteInterrupt() with interrupts held, for example while sending an error message, and then the conflict is never resolved. The author posted a reworked approach on 2025-01-21. No reply follows in the visible messages, and they do not say why the entry was withdrawn.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: Unfortunately I suspect that this means any protection we'd get from this version of the patch is rather incomplete - if the recovery conflict is triggered while not blocked, we'll ERROR out and report the message with interrupts held.

precedents_retrieved.title: Synchronous replay mode for avoiding stale reads on hot standbys
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds a synchronous_replay mode in which a commit on the primary waits until all available hot standbys have replayed it, and the primary grants time-limited leases to standbys. A standby without a valid lease rejects synchronous_replay transactions with a new error 40P02, so reads on standbys never miss a commit that has already returned on the primary.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The visible messages do not show why. The last visible message, from February 2019, is a rebase by the author, and the entry was withdrawn in July 2019. Open items still visible at that point included missing TAP tests, an unexplained replication protocol corruption bug, and design questions from Masahiko Sawada about the GUCs.

roaster_notes.note: No precedent records a reason that applies here. P1's rule allows a timeout set in ResolveRecoveryConflictWithBufferPin(), and v3 adds exactly that. P5 and P9 concern a different wait and a backend blocked in ClientWrite, and their reasons do not carry over to this fix.

The patch adds no syntax, GUC, catalog object, psql feature or dump state, and the 1s interval is a hardcoded define. The one visible behaviour change is in a minor release: a late pinner on a standby is now cancelled about one second after it takes the pin, where before it could hold replay without limit. That matches the documented contract of max_standby_streaming_delay, and Xuneng withdrew the concern that it breaks that contract in message #11. Not checked without the code: whether the wait event shown in pg_stat_activity stays the same during the timed wait.

The proposal adds no persistent or cross-node state. It changes no WAL record, catalog, on-disk format or protocol message, and v3 leaves proc.h untouched, so it adds no ABI concern for backpatching. [P1] needed the startup process to be woken only by unpin or by its own timeout in this wait; a bounded latch wait in standby.c keeps that rule. The cost of the once-per-second broadcast belongs to the performance angle.

The patch adds no new privilege, function, view or setting; it only bounds an existing startup-process wait, and it narrows a denial of service in which any standby user who takes a late buffer pin can stall replay. The once-per-second broadcast while the limit is expired affects only performance, and the material does not show any privilege or information-exposure aspect.

From a maintenance and fit view this is a small, contained bugfix with production reports on 17 and 18 and several testers. The once-per-second broadcast cost was raised and weighed in message #8. [P1] supports a timeout-based wakeup, which this proposal uses, so it adds no objection.

This is a bug fix for a replay stall, and no existing feature fixes it. The thread names two ways out of a stall that has already happened: cancel the late pinner by hand, or run pg_log_backend_memory_contexts() on the startup process. Both need someone to notice the stall first, and Andrey saw 5h41m of lag in message #6. idle_in_transaction_session_timeout ends the idle cursor in the reproducer, but it does not help when the late pinner is an active query. The rewrite-as-loop patch in message #5 does not cover this case either, because its expired path still waits with no timeout. No extension or hook can change how the startup process waits. Duplicate CF entries 6444 and 6445 are a process question, not an existing mechanism.

Demand is shown. Two independent production reports exist: Dmytro saw it several times on 18.4 (message #4) and Andrey saw 5h41m replay lag on 17.11 (message #6). Several reviewers reproduced it, the cost falls only on standbys already in an expired conflict, and the only workaround is a manual superuser wakeup.
